methodology: A combined approach integrating numerical simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics for detailed thermal modeling of wall assemblies and dynamic simulation studies using TRNSYS to evaluate the impact of these materials on overall cooling energy demand was employed.
research_objective: Investigate the thermal and energy performance of various bio-based materials, including banana fibers, straw, Typha Australis, and other composites, in comparison to conventional concrete for sustainable building insulation.

key_findings.finding: Bio-based materials significantly improved thermal insulation compared to conventional concrete by reducing cooling energy demand by up to 31.71%.
Banana fiber, straw, and Typha Australis demonstrated the best thermal performance among bio-based materials tested.
Fiber-reinforced composites made from hemp, flax, or coconuts have high thermal conductivity and can improve both insulation capacity and mechanical strength.
The study aims to assess the thermal performance of selected bio-based materials using a combined experimental data and numerical simulation approach.
Typha Australis, straw, and banana fiber are highlighted for their strong potential in reducing heat transfer and improving indoor comfort.
The study considers key climate parameters such as annual solar radiation and average daily sunshine duration (approximately 9 h) for the site selection.
Peak diffuse solar radiation reaches up to 120kWh/m² in July, which is used for simulations.
